title: Multiple questions in oral proficiency interviews
research_question: What interactional circumstances motivate interviewers in oral proficiency interviews to produce repeated or multiple questions, and how do reactive and proactive multiple-question sequences function in managing candidate comprehension?
methodology: The study analyzes a corpus containing more than 100 instances of oral-proficiency-interview questions and tasks. It examines the sequential and interactional environments surrounding multiple-question turns and distinguishes reactive or vertical repeated questions from proactive or horizontal repetitions. Reactive sequences are examined in relation to observable trouble in candidate uptake, while proactive sequences are examined as attempts to prevent anticipated comprehension or hearing problems. Only the abstract was accessible, so finer details of sampling, participants, transcription, and analytic procedure could not be verified.

key_findings.finding: Interviewers frequently use multiple questions on the same topic both to prevent potential comprehension problems and to react to problems that have already become visible.
Reactive or vertical multiple questions are sequentially tied to immediate problems in the candidate's uptake of the preceding question.
The reactive environments identified include repair sequences, missing rejoinders, and problematic answers.
Proactive or horizontal multiple questions occur in interactional environments judged fragile, where the probability of mishearing is comparatively high.

Because multiple questions may be repetitions or reformulations serving comprehension management, the presence of several interrogatives does not by itself imply several independent answer obligations.

limitations: Only the abstract was accessible, preventing verification of detailed corpus composition, examples, coding procedures, or full analytic argument.
The accessible abstract reports a corpus of more than 100 instances but does not provide enough information to assess representativeness or sampling bias.
The study is qualitative and interactional rather than a computational alignment evaluation, so it does not report precision, recall, F1, or comparable alignment metrics.
The abstract does not establish how often a repeated question receives a complete, partial, or absent answer.
The study concerns oral proficiency interviews, an institutional dialogue genre that may differ substantially from workplace email or customer-service interaction.
No proposition-level annotation scheme or machine-readable reply-to alignment dataset is described in the accessible material.
raw_claims: Managing candidate comprehension is a recurring responsibility of oral-proficiency interviewers.
Misheard or misconstrued questions can interfere with gathering evidence for proficiency assessment.
Many interviewer turns contain several questions concerning the same topic.
Some multiple questions are produced after a concrete comprehension or response problem appears.
Reactive repeated questions can occur during repair.
Reactive repeated questions can follow a missing rejoinder.
Reactive repeated questions can follow an answer that the interviewer treats as problematic.
Other multiple questions are produced proactively before a specific misunderstanding has occurred.
Proactive repetitions occur in environments where mishearing is considered especially possible.
Multiple-question turns can therefore contain reformulations rather than multiple unrelated information requests.
